extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical philosophy and ethics (general readers or scholars studying Aristotelian moral theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and interpreting Aristotle's account of moral mean-states (virtues) and their corresponding excesses and defects — e.g., liberality, magnificence, great-mindedness, meekness, truthfulness, tact. Useful for moral-philosophy study or applying Aristotelian virtue-theory to character description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberality (generosity) / proper giving and receiving
rubrics_metrics.description: A mean concerning wealth: giving and receiving the right amounts, to the right people, and from the right sources. The liberal man spends what he ought and in the right manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrounding explanation distinguishes types of stinginess: those deficient in giving (close‑fisted, niggards), and those excessive in receiving (accepting goods from improper sources or improper amounts, e.g., usurers, brothel-keepers). ‘Base-gaining’ (submitting to disgrace for gain) is characteristic of improper receiving. Liberality is preferable to prodigality in certain senses; errors may be either giving too much or receiving/accepting from wrong sources. Examples/anti-patterns: despots who plunder (wicked, not merely stingy), usurers and brothel-keepers (improper receivers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnificence
rubrics_metrics.description: A virtue like liberality but applying only to large-scale, costly expenditures: fitting, grand expenditure on great objects (public works, festivals, temple offerings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key features: magnitude (large scale), fitness/proportion to the work and to the doer’s rank and means, motive of honour, doing it with pleasure and good taste rather than mere calculation. The work must be proportionate to the expense and done fittingly; one can be liberal without being magnificent. Excess (Vulgar Profusion) spends improperly to show off; defect (Meanness) fails to spend what is fitting and spoils effect by niggardliness. Examples: equipping a trireme, furnishing temples, giving public feasts, marriage expenses. Poor men attempting magnificence are foolish (out of proportion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnificence faults: Meanness and Vulgar Profusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Two improper states relative to magnificence: Meanness (defect) and Vulgar Profusion (excess).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meanness: deficient spending even where great expenditure is appropriate; procrastination and lamenting expense; spoiling effect by skimping on details. Vulgar Profusion: lavishing on small or improper objects to display wealth, spending ostentatiously and in poor taste (e.g., giving actors purple for trivial scenes). Both are faulty because they are either out of proportion or improperly directed, though not necessarily disgraceful in the way that injustice is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great‑mindedness (megalopsychia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimating oneself highly and justly — the mean with respect to greatness of character; one who regards himself as worthy of great honour and behaves accordingly but with moral propriety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great‑mindedness has honour as its primary object; the truly great‑minded are also thoroughly good (virtue is required). Distinguishes from Vanity (excess — overestimating without grounds) and Small‑mindedness (defect — undervaluing oneself). Traits: bearing honours and dishonours appropriately, moderate responses to wealth/power, willing to risk much for high ends, giving kindness readily but ashamed to receive, asking favours reluctantly, reserved toward the many but affable to middling people, preferring reality to appearance, slow deliberate speech and manner. Anti-patterns: those who mimic greatness without virtue (supercilious, insolent) or who are unworthy yet overestimate themselves (vain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Great‑mindedness faults: Vanity and Small‑mindedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Two deviations from great‑mindedness: Vanity (excess) and Small‑mindedness (defect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vanity: undue self-estimation without grounds; sets oneself off by dress, carriage, and talk, attempts honourable things unworthily. Small‑mindedness: underestimates one’s deserts, leads to failure to pursue honourable actions and external goods. Small‑mindedness is more common and worse than vanity according to the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of Honour (the 'lover of honour')
rubrics_metrics.description: An attitude/virtue concerning the desire for honour — can be praise‑worthy when rightly ordered or blameworthy when excessive or from improper sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term can signify different things: when praised it denotes a noble appetite for honour; when blamed it denotes too great a desire or pursuit from wrong sources. The mean state (appropriate love of honour) sometimes lacks a distinct name and sits between ambition and lack of desire for honour. Judgement of praise/blame depends on degree, source, and manner of seeking honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meekness (proper anger)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean state with Anger as its object: being angry at the right people, for the right reasons, in the right manner, at the right time, and for the right duration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praised as imperturbability: anger under the guidance of reason. Defect (Angerlessness): failing to be angry where one ought to be (seen as slavish or foolish). Excesses: Passionate (quick to anger but soon cools), Choleric (excessively vehement), Bitter‑tempered (keeps anger long, hard to reconcile), Cross‑grained (angry at wrong objects and too long). The appropriate boundary is often case‑specific; small deviations are less blameworthy than large ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social intercourse propriety (complaisance / agreeableness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean in social conduct about giving pleasure and avoiding pain in interactions: neither always acquiescing nor opposing everything, but acting according to propriety and what is noble and expedient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess: Over‑Complaisant — always agree to give pleasure and avoid opposing; Defect: Cross/Contentious — opposes in everything regardless of pain caused. The mean resembles an amiable, proper friend: gives pleasure and avoids pain with reference to rank, context, and what is noble/expedient; may inflict small pains for greater subsequent benefits. Distinguishes flatterers (complaisance for gain) from genuinely agreeable persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness (plain matter‑of‑fact honesty)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mean concerning truth in words and life: admitting what belongs to oneself and speaking neither more nor less than the truth in matters not involving strict justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defect: Reserved — depreciates or denies one's merits; sometimes regarded refined. Excess: Exaggerator (inclines to claim credit beyond reality), Braggart (exaggerates for glory), or liars (falsehood for its own sake). The truthful man leans slightly toward understatement in taste; falsehood is base and blameworthy, especially when for gain. Examples of vice: Factotums who falsely claim obvious small things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jocularity / Tact (witty, fitting humour)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mean in joking and jocular exchange: saying and listening to what is fit for a gentleman; avoiding obscene or hurtful jesting while allowing tasteful amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excess: Buffoon / Vulgar — seeks laughter at any cost, including offending or indulging crude scurrility. Defect: Clownish / Stern — will not make or tolerate jokes and is socially rigid. The mean (man of Tact/Easy Pleasantry) knows what is becoming for a gentleman, avoids causing pain, and adapts to education and context (difference noted between Old and New Comedy: obscene vs innuendo). Some forms of jesting may be legally or morally forbidden; tact implies being a law unto oneself in avoiding indecent jesting. Pauses and amusement in life are necessary, but must be moderated.
